Oncomyra.core_claim: Identify FGFR2, act on the evidence, manage with confidence.
Oncomyra.positioning_statement: For oncologists treating previously treated FGFR2 fusion-positive advanced cholangiocarcinoma, Oncomyra is an FGFR2-directed antibody-drug conjugate that delivered a significant overall-survival benefit vs chemotherapy in CLARITY-01 -- supported by fusion-partner-agnostic response and defined management pathways for real-world, comorbid patients.

message_hierarchy.claim: Test every advanced iCCA patient for FGFR2 fusions -- at diagnosis
message_hierarchy.evidence: FGFR2 fusions occur in ~10-16% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and act as oncogenic drivers; RNA-based NGS preferred; a negative liquid biopsy needs reflex tissue testing (REF-01, REF-02)

message_hierarchy.claim: Significant overall survival vs chemotherapy in FGFR2 fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma
message_hierarchy.evidence: mOS 12.8 vs 9.1 mo (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.54-0.96; P=0.008); mPFS 6.4 vs 3.2 mo (HR 0.58; P<0.001) by BICR; ORR 38.7% vs 14.2% vs FOLFOX (REF-01). Open-label design; always with fair balance

message_hierarchy.claim: An FGFR2-directed ADC -- targets FGFR2 from the outside in
message_hierarchy.evidence: Binds the extracellular FGFR2 domain, internalizes, and releases a microtubule-disrupting payload -- a mechanism hypothesized to be less dependent on the kinase pocket that drives TKI resistance (REF-01, REF-02)

message_hierarchy.claim: A known, monitorable profile with defined management
message_hierarchy.evidence: Hyperphosphatemia (on-target class effect) and ocular events managed per algorithm; baseline eye exam + OCT; phosphate monitoring, diet and binders (REF-03). Never present efficacy without balance

Oncomyra.approved_indication: ILLUSTRATIVE / NOT APPROVED. Studied population: adults with previously treated (>=1 prior line of gemcitabine-based therapy), unresectable locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring an FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement (REF-01, REF-03). First-line combination use is INVESTIGATIONAL only. No approved label, ISI, or PI exists in the source set.
Oncomyra.safety_reference: Key signals: hyperphosphatemia (on-target/class), ocular events (dry eye; rarely CSR/RPED), cytopenias, stomatitis, fluid retention/peripheral edema, hepatic monitoring. Fair balance + full ISI mandatory on all promotional materials. Precise AE incidences and all dosing/drug-interaction statements are BLOCKED until source conflicts are resolved against the final PI (see guardrails).

dos.text: Lead the market on 'test at diagnosis' for FGFR2 fusions (unbranded / disease-education territory)
Anchor the branded story in CLARITY-01 OS -- always cite HR + 95% CI + P and the 2L+ FGFR2-positive population
Co-present prominent safety (hyperphosphatemia, ocular, cytopenias, fluid retention) with every efficacy claim, plus full ISI
Present MOA differentiation mechanistically only; keep resistance rationale conditional ('may / hypothesized')
Turn the safety profile into a manageability proof point via monitoring algorithms and special-population guidance
Trace every claim to a reference ID + location; attribute every statistic (VS rate, resistance rate, duration)

donts.text: No 'best', 'breakthrough', 'game-changing', 'first-in-class' or 'standard of care' without regulatory substantiation
No first-line / combination promotion -- it is investigational and medical-only
No superiority vs other FGFR inhibitors -- no head-to-head data exists; only the studied vs-FOLFOX comparison is supported
No survival/cure overpromising; no extrapolation of CLARITY-01 figures to individual patients
No safety minimization; never present efficacy without balance; never use an unqualified 'well-tolerated'
Do NOT publish any dosing, schedule, or drug-interaction statement until the source conflicts are resolved against the PI (blocking gate)
No patient-facing promotional claims until PI/ISI + regulatory framework exist (patient content is gated)

concepts.name: Proven in Phase III. Practical in practice.
concepts.description: Master efficacy platform: pairs the CLARITY-01 overall-survival result with the manageability story so 'proven' and 'practical' travel together. Always with fair balance and full ISI. (Requires MLR.)

concepts.name: If it's advanced iCCA, test for FGFR2 -- at diagnosis
concepts.description: Largely unbranded testing-education platform. Drives universal, RNA-based NGS profiling at diagnosis; a positive liquid biopsy can initiate therapy, a negative one needs reflex tissue testing so eligible patients aren't missed.

concepts.name: Targeting FGFR2 from the outside in
concepts.description: Differentiates the ADC mechanism vs kinase-pocket TKIs; resistance rationale kept conditional. Mechanistic, never a comparative-efficacy claim.

concepts.name: Known profile. Defined management.
concepts.description: Converts the safety profile from barrier to manageability: hyperphosphatemia and ocular monitoring algorithms, special-population guidance, treatment continuity.

concepts.name: One fusion detected -- regardless of partner
concepts.description: De-risks patient selection: response was consistent across major FGFR2 fusion partners (P=0.82), so if a fusion is found the patient may be a candidate regardless of the partner gene.

concepts.name: You are not alone
concepts.description: Patient/caregiver support platform (gated on PI/ISI/reg input). Disease-education and support-resource scaffolding only; no product claims, no outcome language until approved.

concepts.name: First-line combination (FUSION-01)
concepts.description: talrenimab + gemcitabine/cisplatin, Phase Ib/II -- ORR 62.3% vs 41.2%, PFS 9.8 vs 6.4 mo; OS immature; Phase III FUSION-02 planned. MEDICAL-ONLY, investigational -- never promotional.

message_pool: Proven precision, made practical -- identify FGFR2, act on the evidence, manage with confidence
Significant OS vs chemotherapy in CLARITY-01 (12.8 vs 9.1 mo; HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.54-0.96; P=0.008)
If it's advanced iCCA, test for FGFR2 fusions -- at diagnosis (RNA-based NGS preferred)
An FGFR2-directed ADC: binds extracellular FGFR2, delivers a cytotoxic payload inside the cell
Response consistent across major FGFR2 fusion partners (P=0.82) -- regardless of the partner gene
Known, monitorable safety: hyperphosphatemia and ocular events managed per defined algorithm

claims.text: In CLARITY-01, Oncomyra significantly prolonged median OS vs FOLFOX (12.8 vs 9.1 months; HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.54-0.96; P=0.008)
claims.note: Always cite HR+CI+P; 2L+ FGFR2+ population; open-label design

claims.text: Median PFS was 6.4 vs 3.2 months (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.44-0.76; P<0.001) by blinded independent central review
claims.note: BICR strengthens PFS

claims.text: Confirmed ORR was 38.7% vs 14.2% (P<0.001)
claims.note: Open-label -- note assessment method

claims.text: Response was consistent across major FGFR2 fusion partners (BICC1 41.2%, PPHLN1 38.5%, AHCYL1 35.7%, Other 36.9%; P=0.82)
claims.note: Supports 'fusion detected -> candidate regardless of partner'

claims.text: Oncomyra (talrenimab) is an anti-FGFR2 ADC that binds the extracellular FGFR2 domain, internalizes, and releases a microtubule-disrupting cytotoxic payload
claims.note: Mechanistic only

claims.text: This ADC mechanism may be less dependent on the ATP-binding kinase pocket that drives TKI resistance
claims.note: Hypothesis-level -- keep conditional ('may / hypothesized'); do NOT state as proven resistance superiority

claims.text: All patients with unresectable/metastatic iCCA should undergo molecular profiling for FGFR2 fusions at diagnosis
claims.note: Ideal unbranded testing driver

claims.text: RNA-based NGS is preferred over DNA-only NGS for detecting FGFR2 fusions with large intronic breakpoints
claims.note: Don't mandate a named commercial assay beyond source

claims.text: A positive liquid biopsy is sufficient to initiate therapy; a negative result requires reflex tissue testing (do not rule out therapy on liquid-negative alone)
claims.note: Critical safety-of-access nuance

claims.text: FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements occur in ~10-16% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and act as oncogenic drivers
claims.note: Frames the unmet need; keep unbranded

claims.text: Hyperphosphatemia is an on-target class effect of FGFR inhibition and was among the most common AEs; manage with monitoring, low-phosphate diet, and phosphate binders
claims.note: Incidence CONFLICT (42% vs 58%) -- use PI figure only; omit incidence until then

claims.text: Ocular events (dry eye; rarely CSR/RPED) can occur; baseline ophthalmologic exam + OCT and prompt referral for visual symptoms are recommended
claims.note: Incidence varies by source -- use PI figure

claims.text: Cytopenias (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia) and stomatitis can occur; monitor and manage per algorithm
claims.note: Higher with combination -- do not use combination rates in 2L+ promo

claims.text: Proactive phosphate monitoring and defined dose-modification algorithms support treatment continuity
claims.note: Present algorithm STRUCTURE, not a specific schedule, until dosing resolved

claims.text: Renal: full dose if eGFR >=30; reduced starting dose if eGFR 15-29; not recommended if eGFR <15; efficacy maintained across renal function
claims.note: Numeric doses conflict-gated; watch hyperphosphatemia/fluid

claims.text: Hepatic: no adjustment for mild impairment; reduced starting dose for moderate; not recommended for severe; optimize biliary drainage first
claims.note: Moderate HI ~34% higher free-payload AUC; numeric doses conflict-gated

claims.text: Cardiovascular: pre-existing CVD is not a contraindication; main risk is volume overload; negligible QTc effect; no signal of direct myocardial toxicity
claims.note: DDI/CYP conflict with REF-03 -- do not make DDI claims until resolved

claims.text: In real-world use (N=487), median OS was 11.2 months, PFS 5.8 months, ORR 34.1% -- consistent with trial, in an older/sicker population
claims.note: Retrospective; no superiority/causal claims; promo use limited

claims.text: Oncomyra is supported by testing-education, monitoring tools, and management resources

hcp.name: The Precision Specialist (GI / medical oncologist)
hcp.who: Treats advanced iCCA; decides at/after progression on gemcitabine-based therapy
hcp.voice: Show me the CLARITY-01 data and how I identify and manage the right patient -- not just start a drug.
hcp.practice_setting: Oncology clinic managing advanced iCCA patients, focused on applying evidence to real-world patient care.
hcp.goals: Effectively identify and manage FGFR2 fusion-positive iCCA patients; wants clear, evidence-based pathways for patient selection and safety management, particularly for comorbid patients.
hcp.barriers: Concerns about identifying the appropriate patients for targeted therapy and managing potential treatment-related adverse events effectively in real-world settings.
hcp.objections: Skepticism about the differentiation and practical value compared to existing therapies, given the open-label design of CLARITY-01, and potential challenges with safety management.
hcp.message_resonance: The OS benefit from CLARITY-01, presented with clear, practical guidance on patient identification (FGFR2 fusion testing) and proactive safety management algorithms, particularly for comorbid patients.
hcp.narrative: This HCP is a pragmatic oncologist focused on delivering tangible benefits to their advanced iCCA patients. They are evidence-driven, seeking clear data from trials like CLARITY-01, but also demand practical guidance on how to apply that evidence to identify the right patients and manage their treatment journey. They are wary of new drugs without a defined pathway for real-world application, especially regarding potential adverse events and differentiation from existing options.

hcp.name: The Molecular Pathologist
hcp.who: Runs NGS profiling; gatekeeper of FGFR2 fusion detection
hcp.voice: RNA-based NGS matters for these fusions -- and a liquid-negative shouldn't rule a patient out.
hcp.practice_setting: Specialized pathology lab, likely associated with an academic or large hospital system, performing advanced molecular diagnostics.
hcp.goals: To ensure the most accurate and comprehensive detection of FGFR2 fusions, advocating for RNA-based NGS and reflex tissue testing for liquid biopsy negatives, to avoid missing eligible patients.
hcp.barriers: Incomplete or suboptimal FGFR2 fusion testing practices (e.g., sole reliance on liquid biopsy, non-RNA based methods) that may lead to missed diagnoses for eligible patients.
hcp.message_resonance: Emphasis on the critical role of RNA-based NGS for robust FGFR2 fusion detection and the necessity of reflex tissue testing to confirm liquid biopsy negatives, ensuring no patient is overlooked.
hcp.narrative: This expert is the gatekeeper of diagnosis, focused on the technical precision and completeness of FGFR2 fusion detection. They advocate for superior testing methods like RNA-based NGS and are concerned about the pitfalls of less rigorous approaches, particularly the risk of false negatives with liquid biopsies. Their primary concern is ensuring every eligible patient is accurately identified for potential targeted therapy.

hcp.name: The MSL-engaged Academic
hcp.who: Mechanistically-minded; wants design, limitations, investigational context
hcp.voice: It's open-label -- walk me through the BICR PFS and the fusion-partner analysis.
hcp.practice_setting: Academic medical center or large research hospital, involved in clinical trials and advanced research.
hcp.goals: To thoroughly understand the scientific and clinical foundations of the therapy, including trial design, specific efficacy data points, mechanistic differentiation, and the therapy's place in the broader research landscape.
hcp.barriers: Interpreting efficacy data from open-label trials and understanding the full mechanistic differentiation compared to existing therapies, especially concerning resistance mechanisms.
hcp.channel_preference: Scientific exchanges with Medical Science Liaisons (MSLs), peer-reviewed publications, and scientific congresses.
hcp.objections: Concerns regarding potential bias in open-label trial results and any overstated claims, particularly comparative claims against other FGFR inhibitors or definitive statements about hypothetical mechanisms.
hcp.message_resonance: Detailed scientific discussions on CLARITY-01's design and specific outcomes (e.g., BICR PFS, fusion-partner agnostic response), along with the mechanistic differentiation (e.g., ADC approach, hypothesis regarding TKI resistance), presented with appropriate scientific rigor and transparency regarding study limitations.
hcp.narrative: This academic physician is a discerning, scientifically-minded expert who values methodological rigor and mechanistic depth. They engage with MSLs to explore clinical trial design, data nuances like BICR PFS and fusion-partner analysis, and the therapy's underlying biological rationale. While they are interested in innovation, they approach new data with a critical eye, especially concerning open-label studies or claims about resistance mechanisms that are still hypothetical.

Solaraid.core_claim: Solaraid significantly improves overall cognitive function by 35% on the CCFS and reduces chronic cognitive fatigue by 42% in PTCD patients.
Solaraid.positioning_statement: For patients with Chronic Post-Traumatic Cognitive Dysfunction (PTCD) who struggle with debilitating cognitive dysfunction, Solaraid is the first targeted treatment that moves beyond symptom management to restore cognitive clarity and function by addressing underlying neurological impairment, enabling them to reclaim their mental sharpness and live fuller lives.

hcp_messages: The First Targeted Therapy for PTCD
patient_messages: A New Hope for Cognitive Recovery

voice_do: Emphasize hope and a positive future, using terms like 'new dawn' or 'pathway to reclaim'.
Be evidence-based and scientifically credible, citing clinical data and unique mechanisms.
Clearly explain the unique, targeted mechanism of action as 'the first targeted therapy'.
Focus on tangible patient benefits and restoration of function, such as 'reclaiming your life' or 'breaking through the brain fog'.
Use empathetic and empowering language that acknowledges patient struggles while offering solutions.
voice_dont: Avoid language that suggests mere symptomatic management without addressing underlying issues.
Do not downplay the severity or frustration of the patient's current condition; acknowledge their challenges empathetically.

Cablivi.approved_indication: 1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE CABLIVI is indicated for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older with acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (aTTP), in combination with plasma exchange and immunosuppressive therapy. CABLIVI is a von Willebrand factor (vWF)-directed antibody fragment indicated for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older with acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (aTTP), in combination with plasma exchange and immunosuppressive therapy. ( 1 )
Cablivi.safety_reference: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Hemorrhage: Serious and fatal bleeding can occur. Risk of bleeding is increased in patients with underlying coagulopathies or on concomitant antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants. If clinically significant bleeding occurs, interrupt treatment. Withhold CABLIVI 7 days prior to elective surgery, dental procedures, or other invasive interventions. ( 5.1 ) 5.1 Hemorrhage CABLIVI increases the risk of bleeding [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . In clinical studies, severe bleeding adverse reactions of epistaxis, gingival bleeding, upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and metrorrhagia were each reported in 1% of subjects. Overall, bleeding events occurred in approximately 58% of patients on CABLIVI versus 43% of patients on placebo. In the postmarketing setting, cases of life-threatening and fatal bleeding were reported in patients receiving CABLIVI. The risk of bleeding is increased in patients with underlying coagulopathies (e.g., hemophilia, other coagulation factor deficiencies). It is also increased with concomitant use of CABLIVI with drugs affecting hemostasis and coagulation [see Drug Interactions (7) and Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ] . Avoid concomitant use of CABLIVI with antiplatelet agents, thrombolytic drugs, heparin, or anticoagulants. Interrupt use of CABLIVI if clinically significant bleeding occurs. If needed, von Willebrand factor concentrate may be administered to rapidly correct hemostasis. If CABLIVI is restarted, monitor closely for signs of bleeding. Withhold CABLIVI for 7 days prior to elective surgery, dental procedures or other invasive interventions. If emergency surgery is needed, the use of von Willebrand factor concentrate may be considered to correct hemostasis. After the risk of surgical bleeding has resolved, and CABLIVI is resumed, monitor closely for signs of bleeding.

molecule_description.value: 11 DESCRIPTION Caplacizumab-yhdp is a von Willebrand factor (vWF)-directed antibody fragment that consists of two identical humanized building blocks, linked by a three-alanine linker. Caplacizumab-yhdp is produced in Escherichia coli by recombinant DNA technology and has an approximate molecular weight of 28 kDa. CABLIVI (caplacizumab-yhdp) for injection is a sterile, white, preservative-free, lyophilized powder. Each single-dose vial delivers 11 mg caplacizumab-yhdp, anhydrous citric acid (0.18 mg), polysorbate 80 (0.10 mg), sucrose (62 mg), and trisodium citrate dihydrate (4.91 mg). After reconstitution with 1 mL of Sterile Water for Injection, USP, the final concentration is 11 mg/mL, at a pH of approximately 6.5.

dosing.value: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION CABLIVI should be administered upon the initiation of plasma exchange therapy. The recommended dose of CABLIVI is as follows: ( 2.1 ) First day of treatment: 11 mg bolus intravenous injection at least 15 minutes prior to plasma exchange followed by an 11 mg subcutaneous injection after completion of plasma exchange on day 1. Subsequent treatment during daily plasma exchange: 11 mg subcutaneous injection once daily following plasma exchange. Treatment after the plasma exchange period: 11 mg subcutaneous injection once daily for 30 days beyond the last plasma exchange. If after initial treatment course, sign(s) of persistent underlying disease such as suppressed ADAMTS13 activity levels remain present, treatment may be extended for a maximum of 28 days. Discontinue CABLIVI if the patient experiences more than 2 recurrences of aTTP, while on CABLIVI. The first dose should be administered by a healthcare provider as a bolus intravenous injection. Administer subsequent doses subcutaneously in the abdomen. ( 2.3 ) 2.1 Recommended Dose and Schedules CABLIVI should be administered upon initiation of plasma exchange therapy. The recommended dose of CABLIVI is as follows: First day of treatment : 11 mg bolus intravenous injection at least 15 minutes prior to plasma exchange followed by an 11 mg subcutaneous injection after completion of plasma exchange on day 1. Subsequent days of treatment during daily plasma exchange : 11 mg subcutaneous injection once daily following plasma exchange. Treatment after plasma exchange period : 11 mg subcutaneous injection once daily continuing for 30 days following the last daily plasma exchange. If after initial treatment course, sign(s) of persistent underlying disease such as suppressed ADAMTS13 activity levels remain present, treatment may be extended for a maximum of 28 days. Discontinue CABLIVI if the patient experiences more than 2 recurrences of aTTP, while on CABLIVI. Avoid concomitant use of antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ]. Missed Dose Administer the first dose of CABLIVI intravenously before the initial plasma exchange. If the administration of the first intravenous dose of CABLIVI is missed and plasma exchange is already administered, administer the first CABLIVI dose intravenously and administer the next dose subcutaneously on the following day according to the usual dosing schedule. If a dose of CABLIVI is missed during the plasma exchange period, it should be given as soon as possible. If a dose of CABLIVI is missed after the plasma exchange period, it can be administered within 12 hours of the scheduled time of administration. Beyond 12 hours, the missed dose should be skipped and the next daily dose administered according to the usual dosing schedule. 2.2 Discontinuation for Surgery and Other Interventions Withhold CABLIVI treatment 7 days prior to elective surgery, dental procedures, or other invasive interventions [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] . 2.3 Reconstitution and Administration Instructions The first dose of CABLIVI should be administered by a healthcare provider as a bolus intravenous injection. Administer subsequent doses subcutaneously in the abdomen. Avoid injections around the navel. Do not administer consecutive injections in the same abdominal quadrant. Adult patients may self-inject, or adult caregivers may inject CABLIVI subcutaneously after proper instruction on the preparation and administration of CABLIVI, including aseptic technique [see Instructions for Use ] if a healthcare provider determines that it is appropriate. In pediatric patients 12 years of age and older, CABLIVI must be administered by a healthcare provider or an adult caregiver. If the carton was not stored at room temperature, allow the CABLIVI vial and diluent syringe to reach room temperature [25°C to 30°C (77°F to 86°F)] by holding them in your hands for 10 seconds. Do not use any other way to warm up the vial and syringe. Reconstitute CABLIVI before administration using the provided syringe containing 1 mL Sterile Water for Injection, USP, to yield an 11 mg/mL single-dose solution. Using aseptic technique throughout the preparation of the solution, attach the vial adapter to the vial containing CABLIVI. Remove the plastic cap from the syringe and attach it to the vial adapter by twisting it clockwise until it cannot twist any further. Slowly push the syringe plunger down until the syringe is empty. Do not remove the syringe from the vial adapter. Gently swirl the vial until the cake or powder is completely dissolved. Do not shake. Visually inspect that the reconstituted solution is clear and colorless. Withdraw all of the clear, colorless reconstituted solution from the vial into the syringe. Label the CABLIVI syringe. Administer the full amount of reconstituted solution. For the initial intravenous injection, if using an intravenous line, the glass syringe should be connected to a standard Luer lock and flushed with either 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, or 5% Dextrose Injection, USP. Use the CABLIVI solution immediately. If not, use CABLIVI within 4 hours after reconstitution when stored in the refrigerator at 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F).

warnings.value: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Hemorrhage: Serious and fatal bleeding can occur. Risk of bleeding is increased in patients with underlying coagulopathies or on concomitant antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants. If clinically significant bleeding occurs, interrupt treatment. Withhold CABLIVI 7 days prior to elective surgery, dental procedures, or other invasive interventions. ( 5.1 ) 5.1 Hemorrhage CABLIVI increases the risk of bleeding [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . In clinical studies, severe bleeding adverse reactions of epistaxis, gingival bleeding, upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and metrorrhagia were each reported in 1% of subjects. Overall, bleeding events occurred in approximately 58% of patients on CABLIVI versus 43% of patients on placebo. In the postmarketing setting, cases of life-threatening and fatal bleeding were reported in patients receiving CABLIVI. The risk of bleeding is increased in patients with underlying coagulopathies (e.g., hemophilia, other coagulation factor deficiencies). It is also increased with concomitant use of CABLIVI with drugs affecting hemostasis and coagulation [see Drug Interactions (7) and Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) ] . Avoid concomitant use of CABLIVI with antiplatelet agents, thrombolytic drugs, heparin, or anticoagulants. Interrupt use of CABLIVI if clinically significant bleeding occurs. If needed, von Willebrand factor concentrate may be administered to rapidly correct hemostasis. If CABLIVI is restarted, monitor closely for signs of bleeding. Withhold CABLIVI for 7 days prior to elective surgery, dental procedures or other invasive interventions. If emergency surgery is needed, the use of von Willebrand factor concentrate may be considered to correct hemostasis. After the risk of surgical bleeding has resolved, and CABLIVI is resumed, monitor closely for signs of bleeding.

Jardiance.approved_indication: 1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE JARDIANCE is indicated: to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in adults with heart failure. to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease. as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. JARDIANCE is a sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor indicated: To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in adults with heart failure. ( 1 ) To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease. ( 1 ) As an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ( 1 ) Limitations of Use: Not recommended in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. It may increase the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis in these patients. ( 1 ) Not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus with an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ( 1 ) Limitations of Use JARDIANCE is not recommended in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. It may increase the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis in these patients [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] . JARDIANCE is not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus with an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . JARDIANCE is likely to be ineffective in this setting based upon its mechanism of action.
Jardiance.safety_reference: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Ketoacidosis: Assess patients who present with signs and symptoms of metabolic acidosis for ketoacidosis, regardless of blood glucose level. If suspected, discontinue JARDIANCE, evaluate and treat promptly. Before initiating JARDIANCE, consider risk factors for ketoacidosis. Patients on JARDIANCE may require monitoring and temporary discontinuation of therapy in clinical situations known to predispose to ketoacidosis. ( 5.1 ) Volume Depletion: Before initiating JARDIANCE, assess volume status and renal function in patients with impaired renal function, elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics. Monitor for signs and symptoms during therapy. ( 5.2 , 6.1 ) Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis: Evaluate patients for signs and symptoms of urinary tract infections and treat promptly, if indicated ( 5.3 ) Hypoglycemia: Consider lowering the dose of insulin secretagogue or insulin to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia when initiating JARDIANCE ( 5.4 ) Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene): Serious, life-threatening cases have occurred in both females and males. Assess patients presenting with pain or tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, along with fever or malaise. If suspected, institute prompt treatment. ( 5.5 ) Genital Mycotic Infections: Monitor and treat as appropriate ( 5.6 ) Hypersensitivity Reactions: Serious hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., angioedema) have occurred with JARDIANCE. If hypersensitivity reactions occur, discontinue JARDIANCE, treat promptly, and monitor until signs and symptoms resolve. ( 5.7 ) 5.1 Ketoacidosis Reports of ketoacidosis, a serious life-threatening condition requiring urgent hospitalization have been identified in clinical trials and postmarketing surveillance in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving sodium glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Fatal cases of ketoacidosis have been reported in patients taking JARDIANCE. In placebo-controlled trials of patients with type 1 diabetes, the risk of ketoacidosis was increased in patients who received SGLT2 inhibitors compared to patients who received placebo. JARDIANCE is not indicated for the treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus [see Indications and Usage (1) ] . Patients treated with JARDIANCE who present with signs and symptoms consistent with severe metabolic acidosis should be assessed for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose levels, as ketoacidosis associated with JARDIANCE may be present even if blood glucose levels are less than 250 mg/dL. If ketoacidosis is suspected, JARDIANCE should be discontinued, patient should be evaluated, and prompt treatment should be instituted. Treatment of ketoacidosis may require insulin, fluid and carbohydrate replacement. In many of the postmarketing reports, and particularly in patients with type 1 diabetes, the presence of ketoacidosis was not immediately recognized and institution of treatment was delayed because presenting blood glucose levels were below those typically expected for diabetic ketoacidosis (often less than 250 mg/dL). Signs and symptoms at presentation were consistent with dehydration and severe metabolic acidosis and included nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, generalized malaise, and shortness of breath. In some but not all cases, factors predisposing to ketoacidosis such as insulin dose reduction, acute febrile illness, reduced caloric intake, surgery, pancreatic disorders suggesting insulin deficiency (e.g., type 1 diabetes, history of pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery), and alcohol abuse were identified. Before initiating JARDIANCE, consider factors in the patient history that may predispose to ketoacidosis including pancreatic insulin deficiency from any cause, caloric restriction, and alcohol abuse. For patients who undergo scheduled surgery, consider temporarily discontinuing JARDIANCE for at least 3 days prior to surgery [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.2 , 12.3) ] . Consider monitoring for ketoacidosis and temporarily discontinuing JARDIANCE in other clinical situations known to predispose to ketoacidosis (e.g., prolonged fasting due to acute illness or post-surgery). Ensure risk factors for ketoacidosis are resolved prior to restarting JARDIANCE. Educate patients on the signs and symptoms of ketoacidosis and instruct patients to discontinue JARDIANCE and seek medical attention immediately if signs and symptoms occur. 5.2 Volume Depletion JARDIANCE can cause intravascular volume depletion which may sometimes manifest as symptomatic hypotension or acute transient changes in creatinine [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . There have been post-marketing reports of acute kidney injury, some requiring hospitalization and dialysis, in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Patients with impaired renal function (eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics may be at increased risk for volume depletion or hypotension. Before initiating JARDIANCE in patients with one or more of these characteristics, assess volume status and renal function. In patients with volume depletion, correct this condition before initiating JARDIANCE. Monitor for signs and symptoms of volume depletion, and renal function after initiating therapy. 5.3 Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis There have been reports of serious urinary tract infections including urosepsis and pyelonephritis requiring hospitalization in patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors increases the risk for urinary tract infections. Evaluate patients for signs and symptoms of urinary tract infections and treat promptly, if indicated [see Adverse Reactions (6) ] . 5.4 Hypoglycemia with Concomitant Use with Insulin and Insulin Secretagogues Insulin and insulin secretagogues are known to cause hypoglycemia. The risk of hypoglycemia is increased when JARDIANCE is used in combination with insulin secretagogues (e.g., sulfonylurea) or insulin [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . Therefore, a lower dose of the insulin secretagogue or insulin may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia when used in combination with JARDIANCE. 5.5 Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene) Reports of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier's gangrene), a rare but serious and life-threatening necrotizing infection requiring urgent surgical intervention, have been identified in patients with diabetes mellitus receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Cases have been reported in both females and males. Serious outcomes have included hospitalization, multiple surgeries, and death. Patients treated with JARDIANCE presenting with pain or tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, along with fever or malaise, should be assessed for necrotizing fasciitis. If suspected, start treatment immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics and, if necessary, surgical debridement. Discontinue JARDIANCE, closely monitor blood glucose levels, and provide appropriate alternative therapy for glycemic control. 5.6 Genital Mycotic Infections JARDIANCE increases the risk for genital mycotic infections [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . Patients with a history of chronic or recurrent genital mycotic infections were more likely to develop genital mycotic infections. Monitor and treat as appropriate. 5.7 Hypersensitivity Reactions There have been postmarketing reports of serious hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., angioedema) in patients treated with JARDIANCE. If a hypersensitivity reaction occurs, discontinue JARDIANCE; treat promptly per standard of care, and monitor until signs and symptoms resolve. JARDIANCE is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any of the excipients in JARDIANCE [see Contraindications (4) ] .

competitors.name: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i)
competitors.threat_reason: While an alternative for glycemic control, DPP-4is generally lack the broad cardiovascular and heart failure benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors like Jardiance, making them less of a direct threat in specific CV indications.

competitors.name: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs)
competitors.weakness: GLP-1 RA users were more likely to discontinue therapy (HR=1.39, p <0.001) compared to SGLT2i users. Reasons may include tolerance, side effects, glucose control, preferences for oral medications, patient costs, and access to medications.
competitors.counter: Patients using GLP-1 RAs were more likely to discontinue therapy, potentially due to tolerance, side effects, or a preference for oral medications. Jardiance is an oral medication, which may offer a preference benefit.
competitors.threat_reason: GLP-1 RAs are strong competitors for glycemic control and also offer cardiovascular benefits, but may have higher discontinuation rates compared to SGLT2i users.

competitors.name: Liraglutide
competitors.threat_reason: As a GLP-1 RA, liraglutide shares some cardiovascular benefits with SGLT2 inhibitors and is a strong competitor for glycemic control in T2DM with CVD.

competitors.name: Canagliflozin
competitors.threat_reason: Canagliflozin is another SGLT2 inhibitor, directly competing in the same therapeutic class for indications like T2DM and heart failure.

competitors.name: Dapagliflozin
competitors.weakness: Among patients not suitable for gliflozin treatment (36%), the major determinant of ineligibility was the failure to achieve the predefined NT-proBNP inclusion threshold.
competitors.counter: For patients with heart failure where NT-proBNP levels are a determinant of eligibility for some SGLT2 inhibitors, Jardiance's label does not specify NT-proBNP criteria for its heart failure indication, potentially offering a broader eligible patient population.
competitors.threat_reason: Dapagliflozin is a direct SGLT2 inhibitor competitor with similar indications, particularly in heart failure and T2DM.

competitors.name: Sitagliptin
competitors.threat_reason: Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor, primarily for glycemic control, and does not offer the same broad cardiovascular and heart failure benefits as Jardiance.

competitors.name: Sotagliflozin
competitors.threat_reason: Sotagliflozin is an SGLT1/2 inhibitor, providing similar and potentially broader mechanisms of action, directly competing in the diabetes and heart failure space.

competitors.name: Finerenone
competitors.threat_reason: Finerenone is a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with benefits in chronic kidney disease and T2DM, offering an alternative pathway for CV and renal protection, but not directly for glycemic control in the same way as SGLT2 inhibitors.

stages.patient: Patients with heart failure (6.2 million adults) or type 2 diabetes mellitus with established cardiovascular disease are identified in the general population. Many with preclinical HF are not yet recognized.

Patients are diagnosed with heart failure or type 2 diabetes mellitus. Initial treatments are prescribed, but there's a risk of early rehospitalization for heart failure (11% within 30 days) and challenges in achieving guideline eligibility for advanced therapies (13-31% for SGLT-2 inhibitors in real-world T2DM).

Eligible patients are initiated on therapy. For heart failure, some may be deemed ineligible due to specific clinical criteria (e.g., NT-proBNP thresholds), leading to missed opportunities for SGLT2i initiation (36% in one study). For T2DM, a significant proportion (45% in HF) are initiated.

Patients continue therapy over time. Persistence at 12 months for SGLT2i in T2DM with CV risk and obesity is 47%. Discontinuation can occur due to side effects, patient preference, or cost, with GLP-1 RA users being more likely to discontinue than SGLT2i users.

mechanism_of_action.value: 12.1 Mechanism of Action Empagliflozin is an inhibitor of the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2), the predominant transporter responsible for reabsorption of glucose from the glomerular filtrate back into the circulation. By inhibiting SGLT2, empagliflozin reduces renal reabsorption of filtered glucose and lowers the renal threshold for glucose, and thereby increases urinary glucose excretion. Empagliflozin also reduces sodium reabsorption and increases the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule. This may influence several physiological functions such as lowering both pre-and afterload of the heart and downregulating sympathetic activity.
mechanism_of_action.source: FDA label (DailyMed) v1, 20230503 · mechanism of action

molecule_description.value: 11 DESCRIPTION JARDIANCE tablets for oral use contain empagliflozin, an inhibitor of the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2). The chemical name of empagliflozin is D-Glucitol,1,5-anhydro-1-C-[4-chloro-3-[[4-[[(3S)-tetrahydro-3-furanyl]oxy]phenyl]methyl]phenyl]-, (1S). Its molecular formula is C 23 H 27 ClO 7 and the molecular weight is 450.91. The structural formula is: Empagliflozin is a white to yellowish, non-hygroscopic powder. It is very slightly soluble in water, sparingly soluble in methanol, slightly soluble in ethanol and acetonitrile, soluble in 50% acetonitrile/water, and practically insoluble in toluene. Each film-coated tablet of JARDIANCE contains 10 mg or 25 mg of empagliflozin (free base) and the following inactive ingredients: lactose monohydrate, microcrystalline cellulose, hydroxypropyl cellulose, croscarmellose sodium, colloidal silicon dioxide and magnesium stearate. In addition, the film coating contains the following inactive ingredients: hypromellose, titanium dioxide, talc, polyethylene glycol, and yellow ferric oxide. Chemical Structure

warnings.value: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Ketoacidosis: Assess patients who present with signs and symptoms of metabolic acidosis for ketoacidosis, regardless of blood glucose level. If suspected, discontinue JARDIANCE, evaluate and treat promptly. Before initiating JARDIANCE, consider risk factors for ketoacidosis. Patients on JARDIANCE may require monitoring and temporary discontinuation of therapy in clinical situations known to predispose to ketoacidosis. ( 5.1 ) Volume Depletion: Before initiating JARDIANCE, assess volume status and renal function in patients with impaired renal function, elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics. Monitor for signs and symptoms during therapy. ( 5.2 , 6.1 ) Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis: Evaluate patients for signs and symptoms of urinary tract infections and treat promptly, if indicated ( 5.3 ) Hypoglycemia: Consider lowering the dose of insulin secretagogue or insulin to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia when initiating JARDIANCE ( 5.4 ) Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene): Serious, life-threatening cases have occurred in both females and males. Assess patients presenting with pain or tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, along with fever or malaise. If suspected, institute prompt treatment. ( 5.5 ) Genital Mycotic Infections: Monitor and treat as appropriate ( 5.6 ) Hypersensitivity Reactions: Serious hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., angioedema) have occurred with JARDIANCE. If hypersensitivity reactions occur, discontinue JARDIANCE, treat promptly, and monitor until signs and symptoms resolve. ( 5.7 ) 5.1 Ketoacidosis Reports of ketoacidosis, a serious life-threatening condition requiring urgent hospitalization have been identified in clinical trials and postmarketing surveillance in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving sodium glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Fatal cases of ketoacidosis have been reported in patients taking JARDIANCE. In placebo-controlled trials of patients with type 1 diabetes, the risk of ketoacidosis was increased in patients who received SGLT2 inhibitors compared to patients who received placebo. JARDIANCE is not indicated for the treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus [see Indications and Usage (1) ] . Patients treated with JARDIANCE who present with signs and symptoms consistent with severe metabolic acidosis should be assessed for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose levels, as ketoacidosis associated with JARDIANCE may be present even if blood glucose levels are less than 250 mg/dL. If ketoacidosis is suspected, JARDIANCE should be discontinued, patient should be evaluated, and prompt treatment should be instituted. Treatment of ketoacidosis may require insulin, fluid and carbohydrate replacement. In many of the postmarketing reports, and particularly in patients with type 1 diabetes, the presence of ketoacidosis was not immediately recognized and institution of treatment was delayed because presenting blood glucose levels were below those typically expected for diabetic ketoacidosis (often less than 250 mg/dL). Signs and symptoms at presentation were consistent with dehydration and severe metabolic acidosis and included nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, generalized malaise, and shortness of breath. In some but not all cases, factors predisposing to ketoacidosis such as insulin dose reduction, acute febrile illness, reduced caloric intake, surgery, pancreatic disorders suggesting insulin deficiency (e.g., type 1 diabetes, history of pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery), and alcohol abuse were identified. Before initiating JARDIANCE, consider factors in the patient history that may predispose to ketoacidosis including pancreatic insulin deficiency from any cause, caloric restriction, and alcohol abuse. For patients who undergo scheduled surgery, consider temporarily discontinuing JARDIANCE for at least 3 days prior to surgery [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.2 , 12.3) ] . Consider monitoring for ketoacidosis and temporarily discontinuing JARDIANCE in other clinical situations known to predispose to ketoacidosis (e.g., prolonged fasting due to acute illness or post-surgery). Ensure risk factors for ketoacidosis are resolved prior to restarting JARDIANCE. Educate patients on the signs and symptoms of ketoacidosis and instruct patients to discontinue JARDIANCE and seek medical attention immediately if signs and symptoms occur. 5.2 Volume Depletion JARDIANCE can cause intravascular volume depletion which may sometimes manifest as symptomatic hypotension or acute transient changes in creatinine [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . There have been post-marketing reports of acute kidney injury, some requiring hospitalization and dialysis, in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Patients with impaired renal function (eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics may be at increased risk for volume depletion or hypotension. Before initiating JARDIANCE in patients with one or more of these characteristics, assess volume status and renal function. In patients with volume depletion, correct this condition before initiating JARDIANCE. Monitor for signs and symptoms of volume depletion, and renal function after initiating therapy. 5.3 Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis There have been reports of serious urinary tract infections including urosepsis and pyelonephritis requiring hospitalization in patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors increases the risk for urinary tract infections. Evaluate patients for signs and symptoms of urinary tract infections and treat promptly, if indicated [see Adverse Reactions (6) ] . 5.4 Hypoglycemia with Concomitant Use with Insulin and Insulin Secretagogues Insulin and insulin secretagogues are known to cause hypoglycemia. The risk of hypoglycemia is increased when JARDIANCE is used in combination with insulin secretagogues (e.g., sulfonylurea) or insulin [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . Therefore, a lower dose of the insulin secretagogue or insulin may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia when used in combination with JARDIANCE. 5.5 Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene) Reports of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier's gangrene), a rare but serious and life-threatening necrotizing infection requiring urgent surgical intervention, have been identified in patients with diabetes mellitus receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, including JARDIANCE. Cases have been reported in both females and males. Serious outcomes have included hospitalization, multiple surgeries, and death. Patients treated with JARDIANCE presenting with pain or tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, along with fever or malaise, should be assessed for necrotizing fasciitis. If suspected, start treatment immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics and, if necessary, surgical debridement. Discontinue JARDIANCE, closely monitor blood glucose levels, and provide appropriate alternative therapy for glycemic control. 5.6 Genital Mycotic Infections JARDIANCE increases the risk for genital mycotic infections [see Adverse Reactions (6.1) ] . Patients with a history of chronic or recurrent genital mycotic infections were more likely to develop genital mycotic infections. Monitor and treat as appropriate. 5.7 Hypersensitivity Reactions There have been postmarketing reports of serious hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., angioedema) in patients treated with JARDIANCE. If a hypersensitivity reaction occurs, discontinue JARDIANCE; treat promptly per standard of care, and monitor until signs and symptoms resolve. JARDIANCE is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any of the excipients in JARDIANCE [see Contraindications (4) ] .

clinical_studies.value: 14 CLINICAL STUDIES Glycemic Control in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus JARDIANCE has been studied as monotherapy and in combination with metformin, sulfonylurea, pioglitazone, linagliptin, and insulin. JARDIANCE has also been studied in patients with type 2 diabetes with mild or moderate renal impairment. In patients with type 2 diabetes, treatment with JARDIANCE reduced hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), compared to placebo. The reduction in HbA1c for JARDIANCE compared with placebo was observed across subgroups including gender, race, geographic region, baseline BMI and duration of disease. Monotherapy A total of 986 patients with type 2 diabetes participated in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of JARDIANCE monotherapy. Treatment-naïve patients with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes entered an open-label placebo run-in for 2 weeks. At the end of the run-in period, patients who remained inadequately controlled and had an HbA1c between 7% and 10% were randomized to placebo, JARDIANCE 10 mg, JARDIANCE 25 mg, or a reference comparator. Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease The effect of JARDIANCE on cardiovascular risk in adult patients with type 2 diabetes and established, stable, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease was evaluated in the EMPA-REG OUTCOME study, a multicenter, multinational, randomized, double-blind parallel group trial. The study compared the risk of experiencing a major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) between JARDIANCE and placebo when these were added to and used concomitantly with standard of care treatments for diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Coadministered antidiabetic medications were to be kept stable for the first 12 weeks of the trial. Thereafter, antidiabetic and atherosclerotic therapies could be adjusted, at the discretion of investigators, to ensure participants were treated according to the standard care for these diseases. A total of 7020 patients were treated (JARDIANCE 10 mg = 2345; JARDIANCE 25 mg = 2342; placebo = 2333) and followed for a median of 3.1 years. Approximately 72% of the study population was Caucasian, 22% was Asian, and 5% was Black. The mean age was 63 years and approximately 72% were male. All patients in the study had inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus at baseline (HbA1c greater than or equal to 7%). The mean HbA1c at baseline was 8.1% and 57% of participants had diabetes for more than 10 years. Approximately 31%, 22% and 20% reported a past history of neuropathy, retinopathy and nephropathy to investigators, respectively and the mean eGFR was 74 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . At baseline, patients were treated with one (~30%) or more (~70%) antidiabetic medications including metformin (74%), insulin (48%), and sulfonylurea (43%). All patients had established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at baseline including one (82%) or more (18%) of the following: a documented history of coronary artery disease (76%), stroke (23%) or peripheral artery disease (21%). At baseline, the mean systolic blood pressure was 136 mmHg, the mean diastolic blood pressure was 76 mmHg, the mean LDL was 86 mg/dL, the mean HDL was 44 mg/dL, and the mean urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) was 175 mg/g. At baseline, approximately 81% of patients were treated with renin angiotensin system inhibitors, 65% with beta-blockers, 43% with diuretics, 77% with statins, and 86% with antiplatelet agents (mostly aspirin). The primary endpoint in EMPA-REG OUTCOME was the time to first occurrence of a Major Adverse Cardiac Event (MACE). A major adverse cardiac event was defined as occurrence of either a cardiovascular death or a non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI) or a non-fatal stroke. The statistical analysis plan had pre-specified that the 10 and 25 mg doses would be combined. A Cox proportional hazards model was used to test for non-inferiority against the pre-specified risk margin of 1.3 for the hazard ratio of MACE and superiority on MACE if non-inferiority was demonstrated. Type-1 error was controlled across multiples tests using a hierarchical testing strategy. JARDIANCE significantly reduced the risk of first occurrence of primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke (HR: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.74, 0.99). The treatment effect was due to a significant reduction in the risk of cardiovascular death in subjects randomized to empagliflozin (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.49, 0.77), with no change in the risk of non-fatal myocardial infarction or non-fatal stroke (see Table 13 and Figures 5 and 6 ). Results for the 10 mg and 25 mg empagliflozin doses were consistent with results for the combined dose groups. Of 3730 patients, 1863 were randomized to JARDIANCE 10 mg and 1867 to placebo and were followed for a median of 16 months. The mean age of the study population was 67 years (range: 25 to 94 years) and 76% were men, 24% were women, and 27% were 75 years of age or older. evidence.point: Jardiance was approved in the US on 2014-08-01, and with the current date being 2026-10-02, it has been on the market for over 12 years. This time frame suggests it has moved beyond initial launch.

The drug has multiple indications, including reducing the risk of CV death and hospitalization for heart failure, reducing the risk of CV death, and improving glycemic control. This breadth of indications, especially with heart failure and cardiovascular benefits, often signifies a drug that has expanded its utility beyond initial approval for diabetes, indicating a growth phase.
Jardiance is an oral medication, which is typical for chronic primary care conditions.

The primary indications for Jardiance, such as improving glycemic control and reducing cardiovascular events in heart failure, are characteristic of chronic conditions managed in primary care settings.
The pharmaceutical class 'Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitor' (SGLT2 inhibitor) is known for treating chronic conditions like type 2 diabetes and heart failure.

leaks.finding: Of the 5646 participants who had data available for CKM staging (age range, 66 to 90 years; 3271 women [57.9%]), 24 (0.4%) were stage 0 (optimal CKM health), 104 (1.8%) stage 1, 460 (8.1%) stage 2, 3197 (56.0%) stage 3, 1842 (32.3%) stage 4a, and 19 (0.3%) stage 4b. Higher CKM stage was incrementally associated with adverse left ventricular remodeling, worse left ventricular systolic and diastolic function, and greater progression of adverse remodeling by visit 7 (2018-2019). Among participants without prevalent HF at visit 5 (n=4827), the risk of incident HF during follow-up (656 events; median follow-up time, 9.0 years) increased with higher CKM syndrome stage: stage 0/1, 0 events per 1000 person-years; stage 2, 2.9 events/1000 person-years (referent due to no events in stage 0/1); stage 3, 15.1 events/1000 person-years (adjusted hazard ratio, 3.6 [95% CI, 2.1-6.0]); stage 4, 37.4 events/1000 person-years (adjusted hazard ratio, 8.3 [95% CI, 4.9-14.2]; Ptrend<0.001).

Over a median follow-up of 9.9 years, 262 HF events occurred. Within PREVENT-HF categories, preclinical HF measures were strongly associated with absolute HF risk: among those with PREVENT-HF ≥20%, HF incidence rates (per 1,000 person-years) were 9.5 with no preclinical HF and 51.5 with elevated biomarkers plus abnormal echocardiography.

Overall, 66 019 patients were included across 437 sites. Median 30-day and 1-year home-time were 30 (18-30) and 333 (139-362) days, respectively. Only 22.1% of patients experienced 100% home-time in the year after discharge. Rates of heart failure readmission and all-cause mortality 1-year post-discharge were high at 29.8% and 37.0%, respectively.

Of the 6584 patients (92%) in the ASCEND-HF population included in this analysis, 751 patients (11%) were readmitted within 30 days for any cause. Overall, 54% of readmissions were for non-HF causes. The median time to rehospitalization was 11 days (interquartile range: 6-18 days) and 33% of rehospitalizations occurred by day 7. Rehospitalization within 30 days was independently associated with increased risk for 180-day all-cause death [hazard ratio (HR) 2.38, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.93-2.94; P < 0.001]. Risk for 180-day all-cause death did not differ according to early vs. late readmission (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.67-1.45; P = 0.94).

Moderate or severe LA enlargement was significantly associated with total death (hazard ratio 1.6 and 2.7, respectively), CV death (HR 1.7 and 3.3), and HF hospitalization (HR 2.3 and 2.6) but not myocardial infarction (HR 1.0 and 1.4) or ischaemic stroke (1.1 and 1.5). The increased risk was observed in both patients treated with warfarin or aspirin.

For patients with heart failure, the mean readmission rate is 21% nationally and 23% in New York State. Before the pilot heart failure program began, the 30-day readmission rate in the study institution was 28.6%. The 30-day readmission rate for heart failure decreased by 16.6% after implementation of the pilot program.

gaps.detail: Among patients deemed ineligible for gliflozin treatment (36% in one study), the primary reason was failure to meet NT-proBNP inclusion thresholds, which, if excluded (as per FDA label guidance for dapagliflozin and empagliflozin eligibility), would increase eligibility to 86%. This suggests a potential under-utilization based on specific trial criteria not always mirroring real-world applicability.
gaps.who: Adults with heart failure who could benefit from SGLT2 inhibitors but are overlooked due to restrictive diagnostic criteria or specific biomarker levels.

gaps.gap: Lack of persistence with SGLT2i therapy
gaps.detail: Only 47% of Medicare Advantage beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risk, and obesity persisted with SGLT2i therapy at 12 months. GLP-1 RA users were more likely to discontinue (HR=1.39, p <0.001) compared to SGLT2i users, with reasons possibly including tolerance, side effects, glucose control, preferences for oral medications, patient costs, and access to medications.
gaps.who: Patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk, potentially missing out on long-term protective effects.

competition_self.name: Jardiance
competition_self.strength: Reduces the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in adults with heart failure. Reduces the risk of cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease. Improves glycemic control as an adjunct to diet and exercise in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Demonstrated HbA1c reduction (-0.9% for 25 mg) and body weight reduction (-3.9% for 25 mg vs glimepiride at Week 52).
competition_self.weakness: Eligibility for SGLT2 inhibitor trials can be limited in real-world patients (median 13%-31%). For heart failure, a major determinant of ineligibility for gliflozin treatment (36%) was the failure to achieve the predefined NT-proBNP inclusion threshold.

big_idea.text: Jardiance: Comprehensive Heart and Diabetes Protection. Redefining Lifelong Care.
big_idea.insight: Patients with chronic conditions like heart failure and type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease are constantly worried about the cumulative impact of their conditions, fearing preventable events like hospitalizations and even death, which significantly diminish their quality of life and independence. They are actively seeking treatments that offer protection beyond just managing symptoms or blood sugar, aiming for a more secure and healthier future.
big_idea.reasoning: This Big Idea addresses the core insight that patients (Mr. Robert Johnson, Ms. Evelyn Reed) and their caregivers (Mr. Michael Davis) desire not just symptom management but tangible, long-term 'protection' against serious cardiovascular events like CV death and hospitalizations for heart failure. The phrase 'Comprehensive Heart and Diabetes Protection' directly speaks to Jardiance's multi-indication benefits in both heart failure and T2DM with CVD, offering a unified solution. 'Redefining Lifelong Care' reinforces the long-term nature of these chronic conditions and positions Jardiance as a foundational therapy that changes the trajectory of disease. It answers the patient's concern about 'protecting my heart in the long run' (Mr. Robert Johnson) and 'not end up back in the hospital again' (Ms. Evelyn Reed). The 'lifelong care' aspect also speaks to the importance of persistence, addressing the leak of 47% persistence at 12 months for SGLT2i therapy, by positioning Jardiance as essential for ongoing well-being.

draws_on.what: Patients with heart failure looking for ways to improve their quality of life and reduce hospitalizations.
Patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease concerned about long-term health and preventing future cardiovascular events.
Jardiance reduces the risk of CV death and hospitalization for heart failure.
Jardiance reduces the risk of CV death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease.
Only 47% persistence with SGLT2i therapy at 12 months, highlighting a need for sustained engagement.

big_idea.why_not_competitors: Many direct competitors (other SGLT2is like dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) also offer similar cardiovascular benefits. However, 'Comprehensive Heart and Diabetes Protection' leverages Jardiance's established leadership and broad indications to claim a holistic approach that competitors may not articulate as powerfully or consistently. GLP-1 RAs (e.g., liraglutide) also offer CV benefits, but our focus on 'protection' and 'lifelong care' differentiates from their primary positioning often centered on weight loss or glycemic control. The 'redefining lifelong care' component emphasizes a proactive, long-term management strategy, setting it apart from drugs that may be perceived as more symptom-focused or for singular indications.

alternatives.idea: Jardiance: Guarding Hearts, Guiding Futures. For Diabetes and Heart Failure.
alternatives.why_not_chosen: While 'Guarding Hearts, Guiding Futures' is evocative, it's less direct about the 'comprehensive' nature of Jardiance's benefits across both indications. 'Redefining Lifelong Care' provides a stronger sense of transformative, ongoing management, which is crucial for chronic conditions where persistence is an issue.

alternatives.idea: Jardiance: Beyond Blood Sugar. Protecting Your Cardiovascular Journey.
alternatives.why_not_chosen: This alternative is strong for the T2DM with CVD audience but may not fully resonate with the pure heart failure audience, who may not be thinking 'beyond blood sugar.' The chosen Big Idea explicitly includes 'Heart and Diabetes Protection,' covering both core indications equally.

alternatives.idea: Jardiance: Your Partner in Heart Health and Diabetes Management.
alternatives.why_not_chosen: 'Your Partner' can feel a bit generic and less authoritative. It doesn't convey the strong, evidence-based 'protection' aspect as clearly as the chosen Big Idea. It's also less 'ownable' and distinctive compared to 'Comprehensive Heart and Diabetes Protection. Redefining Lifelong Care.'

fit_check.notes: The Big Idea focuses on 'protection' against CV death and hospitalization for heart failure, and 'lifelong care,' which directly aligns with Jardiance's FDA-approved indications to reduce these risks in relevant populations. It also covers 'diabetes protection' by referring to its role in T2DM with established CVD and glycemic control. No claims are made beyond what is supported by the label.

key_risks.text: Assess all patients for ketoacidosis, even if blood glucose levels are normal. Discontinue JARDIANCE if suspected, evaluate, and treat promptly. Consider risk factors before starting and temporarily discontinue for surgery or acute illness. JARDIANCE is not for type 1 diabetes as it increases ketoacidosis risk in these patients. (Warnings and Precautions 5.1)

JARDIANCE can cause intravascular volume depletion, potentially leading to symptomatic hypotension or acute kidney injury. Assess volume status and renal function before initiating in patients with impaired renal function, the elderly, or those on loop diuretics. Monitor for symptoms after starting therapy. (Warnings and Precautions 5.2)
Serious urinary tract infections requiring hospitalization have occurred. Evaluate patients for signs/symptoms of UTIs and treat promptly. (Warnings and Precautions 5.3)
When JARDIANCE is used with insulin or insulin secretagogues, consider reducing the dose of these concomitant medications to lower the risk of hypoglycemia. (Warnings and Precautions 5.4)

Serious, life-threatening cases of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum have been reported. Assess patients with perineal pain/tenderness, erythema, or swelling with fever/malaise. Institute prompt treatment if suspected. (Warnings and Precautions 5.5)
Do not use in patients with hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any excipients (e.g., angioedema) or in patients on dialysis. (Contraindications 4)

( 1.1 ) Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) in combination with pemetrexed and platinum chemotherapy, as first-line treatment of patients with metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC, with no EGFR or ALK genomic tumor aberrations. ( 1.2 ) in combination with carboplatin and either paclitaxel or paclitaxel protein-bound, as first-line treatment of patients with metastatic squamous NSCLC. ( 1.2 ) as a single agent for the first-line treatment of patients with NSCLC expressing PD-L1 [Tumor Proportion Score (TPS) ≥1%] as determined by an FDA-authorized test, with no EGFR or ALK genomic tumor aberrations, and is: Stage III where patients are not candidates for surgical resection or definitive chemoradiation, or metastatic. ( 1.2 , 2.1 ) as a single agent for the treatment of patients with metastatic NSCLC whose tumors express PD-L1 (TPS ≥1%) as determined by an FDA-authorized test, with disease progression on or after platinum-containing chemotherapy. ( 1.2 , 2.1 ) for the treatment of patients with resectable (tumors ≥4 cm or node positive) NSCLC in combination with platinum-containing chemotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment, and then continued as a single agent as adjuvant treatment after surgery.
